summary.title: The Return of a Static Universe and the End of Cosmology
summary.authors: Lawrence M. Krauss, Robert J. Scherrer
summary.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that in the far future of the ΛCDM universe, all observational evidence for the Hubble expansion, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), and primordial nucleosynthesis will vanish for observers within gravitationally bound systems. As the universe approaches a de Sitter state dominated by dark energy, distant galaxies will recede beyond the event horizon, becoming invisible due to exponential redshift. Consequently, future observers will perceive a static 'island universe' containing only their local gravitationally bound group. The CMB will redshift to wavelengths longer than the horizon and be screened by the interstellar medium's plasma frequency. Elemental abundances will be polluted by stellar nucleosynthesis, obscuring primordial signatures. General relativity will not force a conclusion of expansion because the universe will appear inhomogeneous and empty outside the local cluster. Thus, the pillars of modern cosmology will disappear, leading to the 'end of cosmology' and the return of a static universe model, similar to early 20th-century conceptions. This highlights the unique temporal position of current observers, who can verify the expansion and dark energy, a capability that will be lost in the future.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper demonstrates that in the far future of the ΛCDM universe, all observational evidence for the Hubble expansion, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), and primordial nucleosynthesis will vanish for observers within gravitationally bound systems. As the universe approaches a de Sitter state dominated by dark energy, distant galaxies will recede beyond the event horizon, becoming invisible due to exponential redshift. Consequently, future observers will perceive a static 'island universe' containing only their local gravitationally bound group. The CMB will redshift to wavelengths longer than the horizon and be screened by the interstellar medium's plasma frequency. Elemental abundances will be polluted by stellar nucleosynthesis, obscuring primordial signatures. General relativity will not force a conclusion of expansion because the universe will appear inhomogeneous and empty outside the local cluster. Thus, the pillars of modern cosmology will disappear, leading to the 'end of cosmology' and the return of a static universe model, similar to early 20th-century conceptions. This highlights the unique temporal position of current observers, who can verify the expansion and dark energy, a capability that will be lost in the future.

Research Context
Einstein's general relativity led to the proposal of a static universe model by Willem de Sitter. The de Sitter model was initially thought to approximate a low density universe. The model languished after the discovery of the Hubble expansion. Current observational evidence supports a flat ΛCDM universe with dark energy. All cosmological models with a non-zero cosmological constant approach a de Sitter universe.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study examines the practical significance of the ultimate de Sitter expansion. It posits that future observers in bound systems will perceive a static universe. The hypothesis is that evidence for Hubble expansion will disappear. It predicts that observers will be unable to infer the existence of dark energy. The paper argues that the Big Bang origin of light elements will become undetectable.

Methodological Details
The analysis uses the ΛCDM model with roughly 30% matter and 70% dark energy. The dark energy density is assumed to be constant with time. The Local Group is assumed to remain gravitationally bound. Distant structures are driven outside the de Sitter event horizon. The timescale for invisibility is comparable to the longest lived main sequence stars. The CMB peak wavelength is tracked as it redshifts over time. The plasma frequency of the interstellar medium is calculated using electron density. Elemental abundances are extrapolated based on stellar evolution over 100 Gyr.

Procedures And Architectures
The de Sitter metric is defined in a static coordinate system. The scale factor is given by R(t) = exp(Ht). Objects outside the local cluster become invisible due to exponential redshift. The CMB intensity is redshifted by about 12 orders of magnitude. The CMB peak wavelength is driven to a length larger than the horizon. The plasma frequency is given by νp = (nee2/πme)^1/2. The electron number density is approximately 0.03 cm−3. The plasma frequency corresponds to approximately 1 kHz. The expansion factor to reach this state is approximately 10^8. The helium mass fraction is extrapolated to Y = 0.6. The primordial helium mass fraction is Y = 0.25.

Key Results
At t ≈ 100 Gyr, the CMB peak wavelength is roughly 1 m. The CMB frequency is roughly 300 MHz at that time. The CMB intensity is redshifted by about 12 orders of magnitude. The plasma frequency of the interstellar medium is approximately 1 kHz. The expansion factor required to reach the plasma frequency limit is 10^8. This expansion factor is reached when the universe is less than 50 times its present age. The ultimate helium mass fraction after stellar processing is Y = 0.6. The primordial helium mass fraction is Y = 0.25. The ratio of matter to dark energy density inside the horizon is ~10^-12.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Future observers will conclude the existence of a static 'island universe'. They will have no probes of length scales where dark energy dominates. Dark energy is undetectable when its density is much greater than matter. General relativity does not force a conclusion of expansion in an inhomogeneous universe. The universe will appear empty and static outside the local cluster. Observers will infer a finite age but not a Big Bang beginning. The current epoch is special because we can verify the expansion and dark energy.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model assumes the Local Group remains gravitationally bound. It assumes the dark energy density remains constant. The analysis relies on extrapolations of stellar evolution over vast timescales. The visibility of distant objects is limited by the event horizon. The CMB becomes unobservable due to redshift and plasma screening.

Claims
In the far future, observers will be unable to detect the Hubble expansion. Distant structures are driven outside the de Sitter event horizon. Light from distant objects is exponentially redshifted. Only gravitationally bound objects remain visible.  Observers will perceive a static universe.
The Cosmic Microwave Background will become undetectable. The CMB peak wavelength redshifts to larger than the horizon. The CMB is screened by the interstellar medium plasma frequency.  Evidence for the hot Big Bang disappears.
Primordial elemental abundances will be obscured by stellar processing. Helium abundance is enhanced by stellar nucleosynthesis. Relic deuterium is destroyed over time.  BBN evidence becomes difficult to infer.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating the 'end of cosmology' in the far future. 2. The strongest evidence is the redshift of the CMB beyond detectability. 3. The future path is a return to a static universe model.
